summary: Specifies the Neighbor Discovery protocol for IPv6, which hosts and routers use to find each other, learn link-layer addresses, find routers and detect changes. It replaces ARP for IPv6. It was a draft standard, replaced by RFC 4861.

plainLanguage.summary: Neighbor Discovery lets IPv6 devices find routers and learn how to send packets to nearby devices. It also checks whether a neighbor is reachable and whether its link-layer address has changed.

questions: how do ipv6 hosts find routers
how does ipv6 neighbor discovery replace arp
what are the neighbor cache states
subtitle: How IPv6 nodes find routers and neighbors and check whether paths still work.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes on the same link need to find routers, learn link-layer addresses and detect when a neighbor or route stops working.
tldr.mechanism: Neighbor Discovery uses five ICMP message types for router discovery, address resolution and redirects, along with a cache and reachability checks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2461 obsoleted RFC 1970 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4861. RFC 4311 updated it.

today: RFC 2461 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 1970. It has been obsoleted by RFC 4861 and updated by RFC 4311.

sections.title: What Neighbor Discovery Does
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery applies to IPv6 hosts and routers on connected links. It resolves link-layer addresses, helps hosts find routers, tracks whether neighbors can receive packets and detects changed link-layer addresses.

Its jobs also include discovering prefixes and link parameters, supporting address autoconfiguration, determining a next hop, detecting duplicate addresses and delivering redirects. The RFC describes it as combining functions that IPv4 handles with ARP, ICMP Router Discovery and ICMP Redirect.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices use Neighbor Discovery to learn who is on their local link and which router can forward traffic. It combines several discovery and address-resolution jobs in IPv6.

sections.title: Five ICMP Message Types
sections.content:
Router Solicitation asks routers to advertise promptly; Router Advertisement shares router, prefix and link information. Neighbor Solicitation asks for a neighbor's link-layer address or checks reachability, and Neighbor Advertisement answers or announces a changed address. Redirect tells a host about a better first hop.

Messages can carry options such as link-layer addresses, prefix information, a redirected header or the link MTU. Receivers ignore option types they do not recognize. Neighbor Discovery messages use an IP Hop Limit of 255.
sections.plainLanguage: Five message types ask about routers, advertise router information, find a neighbor, answer that request and point to a better first hop. The messages can include extra options.

sections.title: Finding Addresses and Checking Reachability
sections.content:
For address resolution, a node multicasts a Neighbor Solicitation to the target's solicited-node multicast address. The target replies with a Neighbor Advertisement that can include its link-layer address. The sender includes its own link-layer address in the solicitation, so both nodes can learn each other's address.

The Neighbor Unreachability Detection algorithm uses signs of forward progress from upper-layer protocols when available. Otherwise, it sends unicast solicitations to a next-hop neighbor that the node is actively using. The cache records the neighbor and its reachability state.
sections.plainLanguage: A node asks for a nearby device's link-layer address, and that device can reply directly. If a used neighbor may no longer be reachable, the node checks the path before relying on it.

sections.title: Message Validation and Security
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery messages must have a Hop Limit of 255. A router reduces the Hop Limit when forwarding a packet, so this check rejects messages that came from outside the local link.

The RFC notes that a device already on the link can still send misleading information, including forged Router Advertisements. It describes IP Authentication Header protection where a security association exists, while noting that unauthenticated local messages remain a concern.
sections.plainLanguage: The Hop Limit check helps reject discovery messages sent from beyond the local link. It does not stop a device on that link from sending false information.
